title.text: Foundation models: pretraining, post-training, model families, reasoning and multimodal models, benchmarks

objects.text: What is a foundation model, how does it become an assistant, and what does a benchmark score tell me?

Applied AI and Automation  |  Session 6 of 14
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome to Session 6. Last time you saw how a language model predicts the next token, how it is trained by the Session 0 loop, and what sits inside a transformer block. Today we ask how a model like that becomes the assistant you use, what the main model families are, and how to judge claims about them.

You see one task answered by two assistants, recorded, and you read a real model card.

That question gives us three things to be able to do. By the end you can explain pretraining and post-training with a picture each, and tell a base model, an instruction-tuned model, a reasoning model and a diffusion model apart. You can read a model card and a benchmark claim with care.

And you leave with a comparison grid you can use on your own work.

title.text:
Your two hours: most of
the time is your own work

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_plan_11.90x3.95_639f5780.png
objects.alt: The two hours in parts, in minutes

objects.text: You see one task answered by two assistants, then read a real model card yourself.

slides.notes:
To get there we have two hours, and most of it is your own work. The first half hour gives you the big picture of how a foundation model is made: pretraining, then post-training, which includes supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning from human feedback. We cover the main kinds of model and what a benchmark can and cannot tell you.

Then I show one task answered by two different assistants, recorded. After the break you read a real model card on paper and build a comparison grid for your own work.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  What does a language model do, and how was it trained?
2.  What does temperature do?
3.  Why can a fluent answer be wrong?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 5. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. What does a language model do, and how was it trained? Take a moment.

A good answer is this. Next-token prediction: it scores every token, one is sampled and added, and the loop repeats. It was trained with the Session 0 loop on text, where the hidden next token is the label.

Question two. What does temperature do? Say it to yourself first.

A good answer is this. It divides the logits before softmax, which sharpens or flattens the probabilities. Low repeats the top token, high gives variety and then nonsense.

Question three. Why can a fluent answer be wrong? Think about your own work as you answer.

A good answer is this. The model always produces a likely next token. Nothing in that loop checks the facts, unless search or files are added.

If an answer was missing, last session’s take-away sheet or workbook page has it. Now to today.

title.text:
How today connects: what we
already have and what it feeds

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_chain_11.90x4.45_3230f377.png
objects.alt: How today connects to the sessions before and after it

objects.text: Each session is built on the ones before it.

slides.notes:
So where does today sit in the story? The dots along the top are the fifteen sessions, from the map at Session 0 to your plan at Session 14, and the gold one is today.

We already hold next-token prediction and its training from Session 5 and the training loop from Session 0. Nothing today starts from zero.

What today adds is this: pretraining and post-training: that loop at scale.

And it feeds straight into what comes next. Session 7: parameters, file size, who runs a model. Keep that chain in mind, because each idea you learn today is a step on it.

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: A large model pretrained on vast data that many products build on. An LLM is a large language model.
Next-token prediction on a huge text corpus. The result is a base model: it continues text.
Supervised fine-tuning (instruction tuning) and RLHF, which make an instruction-tuned model.
Mixture of experts, reasoning, multimodal, diffusion and small language models.
A fixed set of questions with a score, used to compare models, for example MMLU.
The page a maker publishes about a model: licence, size, uses and limits.

slides.notes:
6 words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Foundation model, LLM. A large model pretrained on vast data that many products build on. An LLM is a large language model.

Pretraining, base model. Next-token prediction on a huge text corpus. The result is a base model: it continues text.

Post-training. Supervised fine-tuning (instruction tuning) and RLHF, which make an instruction-tuned model.

Model families. Mixture of experts, reasoning, multimodal, diffusion and small language models.

Benchmark. A fixed set of questions with a score, used to compare models, for example MMLU.

Model card. The page a maker publishes about a model: licence, size, uses and limits.

Keep those words close. The first idea uses them straight away, so let us begin.

title.text:
Pretraining is next-token
prediction on a huge text corpus

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_library_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Pretraining is next-token prediction on a huge text corpus

objects.text: A foundation model starts with the Session 5 loop, run on a text corpus of enormous size.

runs.text: The text is its own label (self-supervised learning).
GPT-2 read about 40 GB of web pages.
The result is a base model.

slides.notes:
Last session you saw how a model learned to predict the next token: hide it, predict, measure the loss, adjust the weights. Pretraining is exactly that loop, and the only new thing is the size of the text corpus. As an analogy, think of a student locked in a huge library with one game: read a passage, cover the next word, guess it, then check and adjust.

Repeat billions of times. The analogy breaks in one place: the model adjusts numbers, it does not understand the books. Pretraining needs vast data and computing power, so few organisations do it from scratch. The result is a base model, also called a foundation model because many products are built on it.

A base model only continues text. How big does this get?

title.text:
Pretraining at scale is the same loop with
more parameters: 124 million to 175 billion

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_scale_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Pretraining at scale is the same loop with more parameters: 124 million to 175 billion

objects.text: Published figures only. Parameters: weights and biases. Closed assistants publish no sizes.

slides.notes:
Here is the build-up in numbers. In Session 1 you met a small digit network with 1,210 parameters, the weights and biases that training adjusts. GPT-2 small, from Session 5, has 12 transformer blocks and about 124 million. Qwen two point five, one point five billion has one point five four billion, from its model card.

The 2022 InstructGPT paper names GPT-3 at 175 billion. A model with billions of parameters, trained on this kind of text, is called a large language model, or LLM. The loop never changes: predict, measure the loss, adjust. What grows is the number of parameters and the amount of text read.

The bars show powers of ten. I do not state the size of any closed assistant, because makers have not published it. What exactly does the loop push down?

title.text:
Pretraining lowers the average
next-token loss; perplexity restates it

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_formula_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Pretraining lowers the average next-token loss; perplexity restates it

objects.text: Toy numbers, except the first, from Session 5. Perplexity: lower is better.

slides.notes:
Here is the number that pretraining pushes down. It is the Session 5 loss, minus the natural log of the probability given to the true next token, averaged over every token in the corpus. That average is the pretraining objective, also called cross-entropy loss. Take three tokens: days got eighteen percent, loss one point seven one, and two invented tokens.

The average is one point two six. Engineers often quote perplexity instead, which is e raised to that average: about three and a half. Read it as the model being as unsure as if it picked among three and a half equally likely tokens. Lower is better. How does the second stage differ?

title.text:
Post-training turns a base model
into an instruction-tuned model

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_coach_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Post-training turns a base model into an instruction-tuned model

objects.text: Post-training adjusts the pretrained weights with new examples.

runs.text: SFT, supervised fine-tuning (instruction tuning): people write good answers.
RLHF, reinforcement learning from human feedback: people rank answers.

slides.notes:
Reading a text corpus does not teach manners, so the second stage is post-training, and it adjusts the same weights with different examples. In the first step, supervised fine-tuning, people write good answers to many instructions and the model is adjusted towards them. This is also called instruction tuning.

In the second step, RLHF, people rank several answers. The ranking trains a reward model, and the main model is then adjusted to produce answers that score higher. That is a simplification of a longer pipeline. A 2022 OpenAI paper, InstructGPT, found people preferred outputs from a 1.3 billion model post-trained this way over the 175 billion GPT-3.

Post-training can matter as much as size. Let me show you real runs.

title.text:
The same task text: a base model rambles
and an instruction-tuned model answers

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_base_vs_instruct_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: The same task text: a base model rambles and an instruction-tuned model answers

objects.text: Real runs, 6 Nov 2026. Greedy decoding: always the top token.

slides.notes:
Here is that difference, recorded, so you do not have to take my word for it. I ran both with greedy decoding, which always takes the top token, as in Session 5, so the outputs repeat. I gave both models the same task text, about a damaged delivery at Nile Valley Foods.

On the left, GPT-2 is a base model. It has had pretraining only. It behaves as if the text were the start of a news page and writes the company has not responded to requests for comment, over and over. On the right, Qwen two point five, one point five billion Instruct, is a small instruction-tuned open model.

It follows the three instructions: a label, a sum and a reply. That is the gap between a base model and an instruction-tuned model.

title.text:
Three kinds to know: hosted assistants,
open-weights models and small language models

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_families_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Three kinds to know: hosted assistants, open-weights models and small language models

objects.text: Open weights means the learned parameters can be downloaded. Session 7 goes deeper.

slides.notes:
Now you know how a base model becomes an instruction-tuned model, so let me sort the models you will meet. A hosted assistant runs on the maker computers. You send text and get text back, so you check the terms and the data settings. Examples are Claude, ChatGPT and Gemini.

I say nothing about their insides, because their makers have not published them. An open-weights model is one whose files of learned parameters you can download and run. GPT-2 is under the MIT licence. Qwen two point five and Mixtral are under Apache two point zero. A small language model, or SLM, is a language model with a few billion parameters or fewer, small enough for a laptop. Session 7 covers open weights in detail.

title.text:
Mixture of experts: a router sends each
token to two of eight expert networks

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_moe_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Mixture of experts: a router sends each token to two of eight expert networks

objects.text: Only two experts work on each token in a layer, so each token needs less computing.

runs.text: Mixtral, 2024: 8 experts per layer, 2 chosen per token.
Output = sum of gate weight x expert output.
About 47 billion parameters in all, about 13 billion in use per token.

slides.notes:
One design inside some large models is worth a picture. It is called mixture of experts, or MoE. As an analogy, think of a hospital reception sending each patient to just two of eight specialist teams. The analogy breaks: the experts are not human-style specialists. Inside the model, a small router looks at each token and picks two of eight small feed-forward networks, called experts, in each layer.

The Mixtral paper from January 2024 describes this. It reports about forty-seven billion parameters in total, with about thirteen billion in use for each token. Each chosen expert gets a gate weight from the router, and the layer output is the sum of gate weight times expert output, over the chosen experts.

The benefit is less computing per token. The whole model still has to be stored.

title.text:
Reasoning models write out
intermediate steps before the answer

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_reasoning_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Reasoning models write out intermediate steps before the answer

objects.text: They spend extra tokens working in steps, which can help on multi-step problems.

runs.text: The DeepSeek-R1 paper (2025) used reinforcement learning that rewarded correct answers on checkable tasks.
Slower and dearer per answer.

slides.notes:
A different kind of change is in how a model answers. A reasoning model writes a long stretch of working before it gives the answer, like an accountant showing the steps of a reconciliation. Because it writes many more tokens, it takes longer and costs more, but it can do better on problems that need several steps.

The DeepSeek-R1 paper, published in Nature in 2025, describes encouraging this with reinforcement learning, rewarding correct answers on tasks that can be checked, such as maths and coding. I only describe the idea. I do not describe how any closed product works. Session 8 shows when to choose a reasoning model.

title.text:
Multimodal models turn images
and sound into tokens too

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_multimodal_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: Multimodal models turn images and sound into tokens too

objects.text: A multimodal model accepts more than text. Images and sound are cut up and turned into numbers the model can attend to.

runs.text: A photo is cut into patches.
Useful for delivery notes, receipts and screenshots.

slides.notes:
Models can also be taught to take in more than text. A multimodal model accepts photos and sound too. The trick is the same as before: turn everything into lists of numbers that stand where text tokens stand. A photo is cut into small patches, a sound is cut into short slices, and each patch or slice becomes a token-like input the model can attend to, next to the text tokens.

The exact method differs between models. This is why many assistants can read a photo of a delivery note or a receipt. It still makes mistakes, and it can misread a blurry figure. For your own work, test it on twenty real photos before you trust it on the twenty-first.

title.text:
A diffusion model makes images
by removing noise step by step

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_diffusion_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A diffusion model makes images by removing noise step by step

objects.text: The noise pictures are computed here. Diffusion models (DDPM, 2020) learn the reverse path.

slides.notes:
Some models go the other way and make pictures. Image generators of the diffusion kind work with noise. In training, a clean picture is damaged step by step until only noise remains. That direction is easy, and I computed this row myself from a simple picture of a sack.

The model learns the reverse path: given a noisy picture, remove a little noise. To make an image, start from pure noise and apply that learned step many times. The foundational paper is Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models, DDPM, from 2020. One sentence is enough for most executives: a diffusion model turns noise into a picture, step by step.

title.text:
A benchmark is a fixed set
of questions with a score

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_bench_cards_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: A benchmark is a fixed set of questions with a score

objects.text: Facts from the original papers. Chatbot Arena ranks by human votes.

slides.notes:
That is what models are. We now turn to how they are judged, so that you can read a claim in a vendor pitch with care. You will see benchmark scores in every pitch. A benchmark is a fixed set of questions with a score. MMLU, Massive Multitask Language Understanding, from 2020, covers fifty-seven subjects from elementary mathematics to law.

GSM8K, Grade School Math 8K, from 2021, has about eight and a half thousand school maths word problems. HumanEval, from 2021, asks a model to write a program from a description and checks it by running it. Chatbot Arena, from 2024, is different. People vote between two anonymous answers, and the ranking comes from the votes.

Each one measures something narrow and real. Most report accuracy: correct answers divided by all questions, so seventy of a hundred is seventy percent.

title.text:
A benchmark describes the benchmark;
your work is a different circle

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_bench_limits_7.70x4.80.png
objects.alt: A benchmark describes the benchmark; your work is a different circle

objects.text: A high score is a reason to test, and no reason to buy.

runs.text: Ask for the setup: prompt, tries, date.
Some questions may appear in the training text; outsiders cannot check.
Votes can reward style.

slides.notes:
Each of those scores measures something narrow and real. So what does a benchmark not tell you?

It does not tell you whether the model suits your invoices, your clients and your rules. The two circles overlap only a little. Ask how the score was set up, because the prompt and the number of tries can change it. Some benchmark questions may appear in the training text, and outsiders cannot fully check that.

Human votes can reward a pleasant style over accuracy. A high score is a good reason to run your own test, and a poor reason to sign a contract. Your own ten-case sample, scored by you, is stronger evidence.

title.text: Demonstration: one task, two assistants, recorded

objects.text: I will show

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_flow_7.30x3.90_1b27033b.png
objects.alt: Demonstration: one task, two assistants, recorded

objects.text: Watch for

runs.text: The task asks for a label, a sum and a short reply.
Both get the same text and nothing else.
Look for invented promises.
The small language model is not ChatGPT or Gemini.

slides.notes:
A score is a claim, and a test on your own work is evidence, so here is one task answered by two assistants, recorded. The task is the one on screen: a shop owner reports three wet and torn bags, mentions a payment, and asks what we will do.

Both assistants got exactly the same text. Claude answered in a fresh session, with no hints. The other is Qwen two point five, one point five billion Instruct, a small language model that I ran on this laptop, three times. Be fair to it: it is a small model, and it is not ChatGPT, Gemini or Claude.

We score each reply on a checklist, and you watch especially for promises the company never made.

title.text:
Claude kept to the facts; the
small model invented a policy

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_two_answers_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Claude kept to the facts; the small model invented a policy

objects.text: Recorded 6 November 2026. Claude in a fresh subagent session. Not ChatGPT or Gemini.

slides.notes:
Read the two replies on the slide. What did you notice first?

Claude wrote fifty-nine words, apologised, checked the payment against the price list, said the complaint was passed on and asked for photos. It promised no refund or date, because the task gave it none. The small model got the sum right, but then invented a policy. In this run it said the shop owner must pay for only seventeen bags, and asked for a further payment, although payment was already made.

The other two runs invented a waived shipping fee and a replacement. This is next-token prediction from Session 5 at work. Be fair: a hosted assistant of unpublished size against a model of one and a half billion numbers says little about open against closed. Claude ran once, the small model three times.

title.text:
Scored on five checks: the small model
failed four of five in all three runs

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_scorecard_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Scored on five checks: the small model failed four of five in all three runs

objects.text: My own scoring of one task. It shows a pattern, and ranks no product.

slides.notes:
To judge fairly, we score both on five checks. Here is the scorecard, and it is my own judgement of one task. Claude passed all five checks. The small model computed the sum correctly in every run. It labelled the message billing. Billing is defensible, since the message mentions a payment, so treat that row as my judgement and the other four as clearer.

It wrote replies of about ninety to one hundred and twenty words against a limit of seventy. In every run it invented something the company never said, and it never flagged what it could not confirm. One task and three runs prove nothing about products in general. They show why you test a model on your own cases before you trust it.

title.text:
Reading two real model cards:
what is there and what is missing

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_t06_model_card_11.90x4.25.png
objects.alt: Reading two real model cards: what is there and what is missing

objects.text: From the published cards on Hugging Face, checked 6 November 2026.

slides.notes:
A test on my task is one kind of evidence. A model card is another, and every maker publishes one. A model card is the page a maker publishes. Here are two real ones. Qwen two point five, one point five billion lists its licence, Apache two point zero, and its size, one point five four billion parameters.

It lists a context window of thirty-two thousand tokens and over twenty-nine languages, and says the training stages were pretraining and post-training. Its sections are introduction, requirements, quickstart, evaluation and citation, and I found no section on limitations. GPT-2 has a limitations and bias part. It says the model cannot tell fact from fiction and reflects its training data.

What a card leaves out tells you as much as what it says. Now you try reading one.

title.text: Read a model card and ask four questions of it

objects.text: 15 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Take the printed card for GPT-2. Answer four questions with a line from the card.

runs.text: What is the licence, and may you use it at work?
How big is it, and what was it trained on?
What does the maker say it should not be used for?
What is missing that you would want to know?

objects.path: /Users/jothamwambi/Projects/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/Applied AI and Automation - Executive Edition/05 Course Maintenance/Build/figures/x_sheet_5.50x3.55_010efdf2.png
objects.alt: What your finished page looks like

objects.text: You keep: The question sheet with a card line beside each answer.

slides.notes:
You have watched me read two cards; now you read one yourself, on paper, for fifteen minutes, and I walk round. I give you the printed GPT-2 card. Answer four questions, and write the line from the card beside each answer. What is the licence, and may you use it at work?

How big is the model, and what was it trained on?

What does the maker say it should not be used for?

And what is missing that you would want to know?

I have started the example sheet so you see the style. Then tell me one thing you would want to ask a vendor that no card answered.

title.text:
Build your model comparison
grid for your own work

objects.text: 10 minutes
Hands-on, no computer
Fill one grid row for a real task of yours, with two models to try.

runs.text: Write your task in one line.

With your grid started, here is the session turned into a table across the company. Reconciling invoices suits a reasoning model, and you check every total. Drafting replies suits a standard instruction-tuned assistant, and you check for promises the company never made. Summarising CVs needs a private setting, and you check personal data and invented details.

Reading delivery note photos suits a multimodal model, tested on real photos, blurry ones too. Sensitive documents may suit an open model run in-house, and you check its licence and size. Poster images suit an image model, with brand and rights checks. These are starting points and never verdicts.
